newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus president sees EU entry helping dispute.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus president sees EU entry helping dispute.

text.p: Cyprus President Glafcos Clerides on Wednesday said the island's accession to the European Union could help in resolving the decades-old dispute dividing Cyprus.
The European Commission on Tuesday reaffirmed that it would start entry talks with Cyprus in early 1998.
But the decision has fanned the ire of Ankara, which has warned it will integrate the Turkish-occupied part of the divided island to Turkey should the entry talks go ahead.

"Our course the (EU) accession will be a catalyst for a solution to the Cyprus problem," Clerides told reporters as he returned to Cyprus after United Nations-sponsored talks with Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash in New York.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 in response to a brief Greek Cypriot coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling in Athens.

Some 30,000 troops are stationed in a Turkish Cypriot breakaway state that only Ankara recognises in the northern part of the island. The United Nations is trying to reunite the two sides under a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.

Cyprus's accession to Europe is a key area of disagreement between the two sides. The Greek Cypriot-led government, internationally recognised as the only legitimate government of Cyprus, submitted the EU membership bid in July 1990.

The Turkish Cypriots and Ankara say allowing Cyprus to join before a solution on the divided island would be a one-sided move that ignored the wishes of the Turkish north and would reinforce the current divisions between Greek and Turkish Cypriots.
A solution to the Cyprus dispute is not a prerequisite for accession, though it is generally accepted that entry negotiations would be less complex if the problem were solved.
"We want a solution before accession but we do not accept that accession will depend on if the Cyprus problem will or will not be solved," said Clerides.
Turkish Deputy Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said earlier on Wednesday that Turkey would respond sharply if plans to bring Cyprus into the European Union weakened the position of Turkish Cypriots.
"Any step taken in connection with Cyprus which we or Turkish Cyprus do not accept will be more than met by our own steps," Ecevit told a meeting of his leftist party's MPs.
He warned on Tuesday that the Turkish Cypriot north of the divided island would be integrated into Turkey if the EU went ahead with membership talks with the Cypriot government as planned next year.

Clerides refused to be drawn into responding to Ecevit's statements. "I do not attach much importance to this, although we have considered it and taken all necessary measures diplomatically and elsewhere."
